title: The Investor-Ready Story Audit
subtitle: Score whether your founder narrative is clear, credible, and specific enough to raise capital and win clients before you spend a dollar amplifying it.

questions.text: If an investor stopped you in an elevator and asked what your company does, what would come out?

answers.label: I'd start with the problem and spend two minutes describing features
I have a sentence but I adjust it depending on who's asking
I have a clear sentence but I haven't stress-tested it in real conversations
I have a sentence I've refined through investor conversations and it reliably gets a follow-up question
I can say it in under fifteen words and I know which phrase makes investors lean in

questions.text: Pull up your website's first sentence right now. How many adjectives does it contain?

answers.label: Four or more: words like 'leading,' 'innovative,' or 'best-in-class'
Two or three I haven't questioned in a while
One adjective; the rest is specific
None. I replaced them with a metric or a named outcome
None, and the first sentence is a number only we can claim

questions.text: When a first meeting ends and an investor or buyer says 'I need to think about it,' what do you actually know?

answers.label: Honestly, nothing. I don't have a read on where the story broke down
They weren't the right fit. Wrong stage or wrong sector
The product resonated but the category argument didn't close
I usually know which part of the pitch lost them and I've adjusted it since
I rarely hear 'I need to think about it.' The story is built so the objection surfaces in the room

questions.text: When you describe what you do to someone outside your industry at a dinner, what happens?

answers.label: I give a different answer every time depending on how I'm feeling
I have a version but it usually takes 90 seconds to land
I have a clean sentence but I over-explain after it
I say it in one sentence and let the silence work
The sentence reliably gets 'wait, how does that actually work?' and that's by design

low.headline: Your story is still searching for its sentence.
low.text: The test is not whether you can explain your company. It's whether the explanation is the same every time and whether it makes someone ask the next question. Right now you're adjusting the story to the room, which means the story is not sharp enough to stand on its own.
steps: Write one sentence that names who you help, what changes for them, and one number that proves it works. No adjectives.
Say it out loud to three people outside your industry this week and watch where their eyes go flat.
Replace the first sentence on your homepage with a specific number only your company can own.

mid.headline: You have a story. It's doing some of the work but not all of it.
mid.text: The sentence exists. The problem is consistency and precision. When you adjust the story to the room, you're signaling that you haven't found the version that works for everyone. That usually means you haven't tested enough versions yet.
steps: Run your pitch opening through a filter: could any competitor in your space say this exact sentence? If yes, rewrite it around a number or a named fact that belongs only to you.
Pick the version of your sentence that got the strongest reaction in the last six months. Commit to it for the next ten conversations and track the follow-up question rate.
Find the two adjectives you reach for most and replace each with a specific number from your actual results.

high.headline: Your one-liner is doing what it should.
high.text: The sentence is sharp, tested, and consistent. The next move is making sure every other surface uses the same language so a buyer who touches four different touchpoints hears one story.
steps: Audit your five most-visited web pages and count how many use a version of your core sentence versus something written at a different time by someone else.
Test whether the sentence still lands when you remove yourself from the room. Can a team member or advisor say it with the same conviction?
Start tracking which version of the sentence generates a follow-up question versus a polite nod. The data will tell you where to push next.

categories.name: Proof That Only You Can Claim

questions.text: How many of the claims in your pitch deck or on your homepage could a competitor paste into their own without changing a word?

answers.label: Most of them. I rely on category language more than company-specific proof
A few are unique but they're buried after the generic ones
About half are specific numbers or outcomes tied to our actual results
Most claims are specific and verifiable: metrics, named milestones, or real customer outcomes
Every major claim is a number or a named fact that no one in our space can copy-paste

questions.text: When you describe your traction in a pitch or proposal, which version do you reach for?

answers.label: Words like 'significant growth' or 'strong momentum'
A percentage growth rate without the absolute numbers
A revenue or user number but not the before-and-after window
A specific before-and-after metric with a named time window
A two-state number with a time window, and I know which version gets the strongest reaction

questions.text: When an investor or buyer asks what makes you different from a named competitor, what comes out?

answers.label: I explain why we're better in general terms: speed, quality, service
I list feature differences
I name one outcome we deliver that competitors don't claim
I have a specific number or a named customer proof point that makes the comparison concrete
I reframe the comparison. I explain which category we actually belong in and why the competitor comparison is wrong

low.headline: Your proof points are working against you.
low.text: Words like 'leading' and 'innovative' cost nothing to write, which is exactly why a reader's brain files them as noise. A specific number does something no adjective can: it's yours and no one else can claim it. Right now your story is generic enough that a competitor could swap in their name and it would still make sense.
steps: Go through your deck and mark every sentence a competitor could say unchanged. Rewrite each one around a real number from your results: users, revenue, time saved, clients named.
Find the one metric in your business that is most surprising when said out loud. Build your traction slide around that number with a before, an after, and a time window.
Replace 'we are the leading...' with the specific two-state number you own. A small number told truthfully beats a large claim told vaguely.

mid.headline: You have real proof. It's not in the right position yet.
mid.text: The numbers exist but they're not the first thing an investor or buyer sees. Proof buried after three paragraphs of category context has already lost half the room. The founders I see get funded lead with the number and explain it after.
steps: Move your strongest specific number to the first 30 seconds of your pitch and the first sentence of your deck. Everything else is context.
Think through your last three investor meetings: which number made someone lean forward? Make that number louder in the next one.
Build a proof inventory: a list of every specific, dated, verifiable metric your company owns. You probably have more than you're using.

high.headline: Your proof is specific and yours. Keep it current.
high.text: You've traded adjectives for numbers. The risk now is that your best proof points go stale. A number from 18 months ago is still a number, but it doesn't do the same work as one from last quarter. The story needs fresh ammunition on the same schedule your product ships.
steps: Set a quarterly reminder to audit your three headline proof points and replace any older than six months with a fresher version.
Find one number you've never used in a pitch and test it in your next meeting. Proof inventories have hidden facts founders skip because they don't feel big enough.
Add a second proof point about the category itself. The story gets stronger when your company proof and your market proof are both specific.

questions.text: If an investor asked why your category is inevitable in the next 18 months, separate from your company's performance, how ready is your answer?

answers.label: I'd explain our product roadmap. I haven't framed a category argument yet
I have a market size number but not a structural reason why now
I have one structural reason but it's the same one every competitor in my space cites
I have two or three specific tailwinds tied to this cycle and I can name them fast
My 'why now' includes a market force, a buyer behavior shift, and a closing window. I've tested it in real conversations

questions.text: How does your narrative handle the AI question honestly and specifically?

answers.label: AI doesn't touch our product and I skip the topic entirely
We mention AI because it helps conversations but the connection to our product is thin
AI touches our product but I haven't articulated how it changes the outcome for customers
I lead with a specific AI application in the product and can describe the concrete outcome it produces
I have a precise explanation of exactly where AI changes our unit economics or delivery speed, and investors haven't found a hole in it

questions.text: When a deal goes quiet after a strong first meeting, what does your story say about the cost of waiting?

answers.label: I follow up with a feature update or a request to reschedule
I mention a round closing or a deadline on our end
I point to a recent market trend or a news article
I have a conversation about what they specifically lose by waiting, in their business
I have a 'cost of delay' argument with a number they can calculate for their own situation, and I know which version ends the pause

low.headline: Growing 3x doesn't close rounds on its own anymore.
low.text: Every founder in a live deal has a growth number. The ones getting checks can also articulate why their category is inevitable right now. Your story is leading with company performance and skipping the category argument. Investors will find that gap before you do.
steps: Write a 'why now' paragraph that has nothing to do with your company's traction. Name the market force, the buyer behavior shift, and the window. Keep it under five sentences.
Find the one structural change in your market in the last 18 months that your company is built to catch. If you can't name it fast, your investors will catch the absence.
Read your last five investor emails and count how many led with company performance versus category momentum. Start leading with category.

mid.headline: The category argument is there. It's not differentiated enough yet.
mid.text: You have a 'why now.' The problem is it's the same one your competitors are using. When every founder in a space cites the same tailwind, it becomes a category story. Investors need to hear why this company wins the category that is already becoming inevitable.
steps: Find the specific version of the market shift that only your product is built for. The tailwind everyone sees plus the angle no one else has is the argument.

Add a buyer behavior data point that is current, specific, and surprising. A behavioral fact that tells an investor something they didn't already know about how buyers are changing is stronger than a TAM slide.
Test the 'why now' argument in your next five conversations and track which version makes someone ask 'who else is in this space?' That question means the category argument landed.

high.headline: You can articulate why now. Make sure the story ages well.
high.text: The category argument is working. The risk is that timing arguments have a shelf life. What made your 'why now' compelling twelve months ago may not land the same way today. A stale urgency argument is worse than none because it signals you haven't updated your read of the market.
steps: Revisit your 'why now' argument every quarter. Ask whether the tailwind you named is still moving or whether it's already priced in by the market.
Add a second layer: not just why the category is inevitable, but why the window for early entry is closing. Timing arguments are stronger when they point to a closing door.

Record yourself making the 'why now' argument cold, without notes, in under 90 seconds. If you can't do it cleanly, the argument is still too dependent on setup context to land in a cold conversation.

questions.text: Where does the majority of your thought leadership content live right now?

answers.label: Our company page. I post there consistently but rarely from my personal profile
Split roughly equally between my profile and the company page
Mostly my personal profile but the posts are usually company news and product announcements
My personal profile, with a real point of view or a lesson from the work in most posts
My personal profile, and I can trace which specific posts generated which discovery calls

questions.text: When a warm lead converts without a cold intro, how did they first encounter you?

answers.label: A cold email or outreach sequence from our team
A paid ad or sponsored post
A company page post or a press mention
A personal post I wrote or a talk I gave
They'd been following me personally for weeks or months before they ever reached out

questions.text: How do you measure whether a piece of content worked?

answers.label: Impressions and likes. The numbers the platform shows on the dashboard
Follower growth or comment count
Profile views and connection requests in the 48 hours after publishing
Whether it generated a reply, a DM, or a warm introduction worth having
Whether it booked a call. I know which posts in my last ten generated a real conversation

questions.text: In your last ten posts, how many generated a discovery call or a meaningful investor conversation?

answers.label: I haven't tracked it. I measure success by engagement rate
A couple did well but I couldn't trace a call back to a specific post
One or two out of ten led to a conversation worth having
Three or four out of ten led to a DM or a scheduled call
I know exactly which posts convert and at what rate, and I use that to decide what to publish next

low.headline: You are the distribution. The brand page is what you send people to after they already trust you.
low.text: Company pages hit roughly 5% of the feed and that reach has dropped about 60% since 2024. The posts that book calls come from a face and a name. Right now you're optimizing the scoreboard that feels like progress instead of the one that actually grows the business.
steps: Pause all company page posting for 30 days and put that energy into your personal profile. Track whether anything changes in inbound quality.
Post once this week from your personal profile with a real opinion or a lesson from a hard week. Watch what happens to DMs versus a typical company post.
Pull your last 30 days of content and count the posts with your face and your name on them. If it's fewer than 60% of total output, you have a distribution problem.

mid.headline: You're posting from your profile. You're measuring the wrong scoreboard.
mid.text: The impressions number is immediate and visible. A post that hit 200,000 impressions and booked zero calls is a vanity win. A post that got 1,100 views and booked three calls is the business growing. Right now the impressions number is probably running your strategy.
steps: Open your last ten posts and add a column for calls or conversations generated. Actual conversations, not DMs that went nowhere. That number is your real content metric.
Find the post in your history with the best conversion rate rather than the best engagement rate. Study what it did differently and write five posts that match that structure.
Before you publish, name the specific person you want to reach and what you want them to do after reading. If you can't name it, don't publish yet.

high.headline: You're building the warm room before the cold email. That's the right order.
high.text: The founders I watch get funded in tough environments almost always share one thing: an audience that already knows them before the cold email lands. You're doing this. The next move is making the content do more of the closing work so you're not rebuilding trust in every first call.
steps: Add one piece of content per month designed to answer the first objection investors or buyers raise in early conversations. Let the content do that work before the call.
Identify your top three posts by conversion rate and find the common thread. Build a rhythm that repeats that structure every few weeks with fresh material.

Make your bio and pinned content do the job of a first meeting. Someone who reads three things on your profile should know what you do, who you do it for, and one proof point without scheduling a call to find out.

cta.headline: Want a partner who turns this score into an actual plan?
cta.description: In 30 minutes I'll show you which two gaps to fix first, based on your score and your stage. No pitch deck, just the sequencing.

persona_selector.text: Which of these fits where you are right now?

answers.label: Pre-raise: building the story before I go out
Active raise: in conversations with investors now
Post-raise: funded and need to win clients
Both: raising and selling at the same time
